name: cargo-nextest (test runner)
baseline: cargo test (libtest), which runs test binaries one after another
verdict_reason: On nine real projects pinned to specific commits, nextest ran the same tests 1.37x to 3.38x faster than cargo test, with commands and hardware published. The gain comes from running tests from different binaries in parallel, so it shrinks for projects with a single test binary.
tier_reason: Projects, revisions, commands, hardware and Rust version are all published, so the runs can be repeated; the numbers are first-party.
claimed_speedup: 1.37x to 3.38x faster test runs: crucible 5.14 s vs 1.52 s (3.38x), tokio 24.27 s vs 11.60 s (2.09x), omicron 444.08 s vs 202.50 s (2.19x), penumbra 125.38 s vs 90.96 s (1.37x)
workload: Test execution only (build excluded) for 9 workspaces with 113 to 1138 tests each; minimum of runs 3-5; doctests excluded
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 16 cores/32 threads, 64 GB RAM
install: cargo install --locked cargo-nextest (or a pre-built binary)
one_liner: Test runner that runs every test in its own process from one global pool; 1.4x-3.4x faster than cargo test on nine real projects.
how_it_is_fast: cargo test runs each test binary in turn, so a slow binary holds up all the others. nextest lists the tests in every binary first, then runs each test as its own process from a single shared pool, so slow tests in different binaries overlap.
use_it_when: Workspaces with many crates and test binaries
Suites where a few long-running tests sit in different binaries
CI pipelines where test time is a large share of the total
skip_it_when: Doctests: nextest does not run them, so keep cargo test --doc
Tests that depend on sharing in-process state with other tests in the same binary
Small single-binary projects, where the project itself says runs may not get faster
caveats: Excludes build time, which often dominates CI runs
tradeoffs: One process per test adds per-test startup cost
Separate install; doctests need a second command

evidence.quote: The measurements do not include time taken to build the tests. To ensure that, each command was run 5 times in succession. The measurement recorded is the minimum of runs 3, 4 and 5.
Even if nextest doesn't result in faster test runs, you may find it useful for identifying test bottlenecks, for its user interface, or for its other features.
